question.text: Given the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2y+y^2-xz$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(2,-1,-1).$
question.explanation:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be expressed as

\[ \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle = 0. \]

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(x_0,y_0,z_0) = (2,-1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla\! f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} ( x^2y+y^2-xz) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (x^2y+y^2-xz) \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} ( x^2y+y^2-xz) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= (2xy-z) \ \mathbf i + (x^2+2y) \ \mathbf j -x\mathbf k \\[10pt] \nabla\! f(2,-1,-1) &= \left(\, 2(2)(-1)- (-1) \,\right) \ \mathbf i + \left(\, 2^2+2(-1)\, \right)\ \mathbf j - 2\mathbf k \\[5pt] &= -3 \, \mathbf i + 2 \, \mathbf j - 2\, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle -3, 2, -2 \rangle \end{align*}

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \nabla f(2,-1,-1) \cdot \langle x-2, \: y+1, \: z+1 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \langle -3, 2, -2 \rangle \cdot \langle x-2, \: y+1, \: z+1 \rangle & = 0 %e(x-1)+e(y-1)-(z-e) & = 0 \\[3pt] %ex + ey - z - e & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Given the function $f(x,y,z) = 2ye^x-e^z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,-1).$
question.explanation:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be expressed as

\[ \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle = 0. \]

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(x_0,y_0,z_0) = (1,1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla\! f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (2ye^x-e^z) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (2ye^x-e^z) \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (2ye^x-e^z) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2ye^x \ \mathbf i + 2e^x \ \mathbf j - e^z\mathbf k \\[10pt] \nabla\! f(1,1,-1) &= 2(1)e \ \mathbf i + 2e \ \mathbf j - e^{-1} \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2e \, \mathbf i + 2e \, \mathbf j - e^{-1} \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \left\langle 2e, 2e,- \dfrac 1 e \right\rangle \end{align*}

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \nabla f(1,1,-1) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z+1 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \left\langle 2e, 2e,- \dfrac 1e\right\rangle \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z+1 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] 2ex + 2ey -\dfrac ze-4e-\dfrac 1e & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Given the function $f(x,y,z) = xyz -z^2$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(2,3,1).$
question.explanation:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be expressed as

\[ \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle = 0. \]

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(x_0,y_0,z_0) = (2,3,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla\! f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} ( xyz -z^2) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} ( xyz -z^2) \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} ( xyz -z^2) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= yz \ \mathbf i + xz \ \mathbf j + (xy - 2z) \mathbf k \\[10pt] \nabla\! f(2,3,1) &= (3)(1) \ \mathbf i + 2(1) \ \mathbf j + (2(3) -2(1)) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 3 \, \mathbf i + 2 \, \mathbf j + 4 \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle 3, 2, 4 \rangle \end{align*}

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \nabla f(2,3,1) \cdot \langle x-2, \: y-3, \: z-1 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \langle 3, 2, 4 \rangle \cdot \langle x-2, \: y-3, \: z-1 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] 3(x-2)+ 2(y-3)+ 4(z-1) & = 0 \\[3pt] 3x +2y + 4z - 16& = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the surface $e^{xy} - x^2 - 2z^2 = e - 3.$ Given that $\mathbf{n} = \langle a,b,c \rangle $ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(1, 1, -1),$ what is the value of $\dfrac{a-b}{c}?$
question.explanation:
Let's define $f(x,y,z) = e^{xy} - x^2 - 2z^2.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z) = e - 3.$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^{xy} - x^2 - 2z^2 \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{xy} - x^2 - 2z^2)\right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( e^{xy} - x^2 - 2z^2\right) \mathbf k\\[5pt] &= \left(ye^{xy} - 2x \right) \mathbf i + \left( xe^{xy} \right) \mathbf j + \left(-4z \right) \mathbf k\\[10pt] \nabla f(1, 1, -1) &= ((1)e^{(1)(1)} - 2(1))\ \mathbf i + (1)e^{(1)(1)} \ \mathbf j + (-4)(-1) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= (e-2)\ \mathbf i + e \ \mathbf j + 4 \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \left\langle e-2,\: e, \: 4 \right\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, our normal vector is $\mathbf{n} = \langle a,b,c \rangle = \left\langle e -2,\: e , \: 4 \right\rangle.$

Finally, $\dfrac{a-b}{c} = \dfrac{(e-2) - e}{4}=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

question.text: Consider the surface $z^2y +16= 4\sqrt{x} + y.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(4, -1,3).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

\begin{align*} z^2y +16&= 4\sqrt{x} + y. \\[3pt] z^2y - 4\sqrt{x} - y&= -16 \end{align*}

If we set $f(x,y,z) =z^2y - 4\sqrt{x} - y$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-16.$

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be expressed as

\[ \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle = 0. \]

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,-1,3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla\! f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (z^2y - 4\sqrt{x} - y) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (z^2y - 4\sqrt{x} - y) \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (z^2y - 4\sqrt{x} - y) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} \ \mathbf i +(z^2-1) \ \mathbf j + 2zy\ \mathbf k \\[10pt] \nabla\! f(4,-1,3) &= -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4}} \ \mathbf i + (3^2 -1) \ \mathbf j + 2(3)(-1) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= - \, \mathbf i + 8\ \mathbf j - 6 \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle -1, 8, -6 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \nabla f(4,-1,3) \cdot \langle x-4, \: y+1, \: z-3 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \langle -1, 8, -6 \rangle \cdot \langle x-4, \: y+1, \: z-3 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] -(x-4)+ 8(y+1) -6(z-3) & = 0 \\[3pt] - x + 8y - 6z + 30 & = 0 \end{align*}
